draft.draft_body: {"type":"doc","content":[{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"There is something it is like to be you. You know it from the inside, more surely than you know anything else. And yet no one can say what it is."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"We can watch your brain light up when you feel something. We can change it, and you change. And still, the feeling itself stays private. This is the old question, and there is a word for it now: the hard problem of consciousness. The puzzle of how a physical thing can have an inside."}]},{"type":"captionedImage","content":[{"type":"image2","attrs":{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/cdd856ea-95e1-42b1-a2ff-50ec25b2f898_1024x1024.webp","alt":"The question of consciousness"}},{"type":"caption","content":[{"type":"text","text":"One is what the brain does. The other is what everything appears in. That is the gap."}]}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"What science can tell us"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Science has done something astonishing here. Every thought, every feeling, every moment of seeing is tied to the brain. Damage the brain and you change the person. David Eagleman has shown this again and again. Scanners let us watch the patterns of a feeling as they happen, and the picture gets clearer every year."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"But there is a step the method cannot take. How does a pattern of cells become the taste of coffee, or the ache of grief? This is what David Chalmers gave a name to. Not how the brain works. Why any of it feels like something at all."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"You can say the feeling is the brain activity, and nothing more. That may be true. But it does not answer the question. It just moves it. It says the two are the same thing, without saying how a thing that moves and fires can also ache."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"What the old teaching says"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Advaita Vedanta starts from the other end. It does not begin with the brain and try to reach experience. It begins with experience. The fact that there is an awareness in which everything appears: thoughts, feelings, the world, your own body. It asks what that awareness is, before it is anything else."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Swami Sarvapriyananda puts the heart of it simply. The mind is an instrument of experience, not the experiencer. You are not your thoughts. You are the one who notices them."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"This is not a theory to believe. It is a thing to look at directly, through a practice called self-inquiry. Ask who is experiencing this. Keep asking. Let the asking turn back on itself. What you find, the teaching says, is that the one who is aware and the awareness itself are the same thing."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Where they seem to agree"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Both sides say consciousness is the deepest thing there is. On the surface, that sounds like agreement. But the words are doing different work."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"When science says consciousness is the deepest thing, it means it is important enough to study for another hundred years. When the old teaching says it is the deepest thing, it means it is there before matter. One is a plan for research. The other is a claim about what is real. Those are not the same sentence."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Where they truly differ"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The difference is about you. Science says there is a body that makes a self, and asks how. The old teaching says the self never had to be made, and asks why we keep looking for it in the body."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Both have something to offer. Science gives us medicines. It treats depression and anxiety by working on the brain it can now partly reach. The old teaching offers a different kind of relief. When you stop seeing yourself as separate, a great deal of the pain that separates you from everything else falls away. One works on the brain. The other works on the mistake."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Neither one is a rival to the other. They are two honest answers to two different questions. And the gap between them is not a failure. It is the place where both run out, and where the mystery is allowed to stay a mystery."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"We may never close that gap. That is not a reason to stop trying, and it is not a reason to pretend it is not there."}]}]}
